chapters.title: Chapter 9: Capstone: Running a Market Making Book Through a Volatile Month

lessons.title: Week One: Ordinary Two-Way Flow and Steady Spread Capture

body.text: Week one is not exciting, and that is exactly the point. A good baseline week is proof the core plumbing works before anything genuinely stresses it.

children.text: Monday to Wednesday: The Core Loop, Running as Designed

The book's first three sessions run exactly as Chapter 1 through Chapter 3 described. Bids and asks sit continuously around a reservation price that barely moves away from the mid, because incoming flow is genuinely two-way and inventory oscillates in a narrow band around zero rather than building in one direction. Spreads stay close to what pure order processing and a modest inventory component would predict, since there is little reason yet for adverse selection cost to be elevated. Fills happen at a steady, unremarkable pace, and the desk's reservation price and skew logic barely has to do any real work, because nothing is pushing inventory hard enough in either direction to require it.
Thursday: A Scheduled Wobble, Handled Routinely

Thursday brings a scheduled macro data release, nothing as significant as an RBI policy decision, but enough to be on the desk's calendar. The book follows Chapter 4's final lesson almost mechanically: spreads widen gradually in the run-up to the release, widen further at the moment of release itself, and narrow back down over the following half hour as VPIN readings on the contract fall back toward normal. Nothing about this requires an aggressive unwind or any real drama; it is the calendar-based playbook working exactly as designed, a useful contrast with what week two brings.
Friday: Closing Out Week One's Numbers

body.caption: Week one's metrics, using Chapter 6's framework

body.text: Notice the average holding time, around 14 minutes, lands close to the 15-minute target the desk designed into its 300-unit inventory limit back in the previous lesson, using Little's Law. That is a small but genuine confirmation that the setup decisions were reasonably calibrated to how this instrument actually trades, not just a number picked in the abstract.

body.title: Confirming the Week's Holding Time
body.prompt: Over the week, the desk's average observed inventory was 50 units, and its average observed throughput was 200 units per hour. Using Little's Law, what average holding time does this imply, in minutes?
body.explanation: W = L ÷ λ = 50 ÷ 200 = 0.25 hours = 15 minutes, landing almost exactly on the target the desk designed for in the previous lesson. This is a reassuring sign for week one, though Chapter 6's own case study is a reminder that a calm week's numbers, on their own, cannot yet prove the setup will hold up once real stress arrives.

body.title: Does Week One Prove Anything?
body.scenario: A colleague looks at week one's results, an 83% spread capture rate, a comfortably positive P&L, and a worst single-session loss nowhere near the kill switch threshold, and suggests the desk has clearly found a working edge.
body.prompt: Using Chapter 6's own case study on telling a genuine edge from a lucky quarter, how should the desk actually interpret week one's results at this stage?
body.modelAnswer: Week one's results are a genuinely good sign that the core plumbing, quoting logic, inventory limits, and the calendar-based event playbook, are all functioning as designed, but they do not yet prove a genuine edge, for exactly the reason Chapter 6's case study made explicit: a calm period, even one with a mild scheduled event handled well, has not actually tested the book against real adverse selection or a genuine one-sided shock. The honest interpretation is that week one has passed a basic functioning test, not a stress test, and the desk should withhold judgement on whether it has a durable edge until it sees how these same metrics behave under real pressure.

body.title: What Week One Actually Demonstrated
body.question: What is the most accurate description of what week one's results demonstrate?
options: Definitive proof of a genuine, durable trading edge
That the core system works as designed under calm conditions, without yet being tested by real stress
That the desk's risk limits were set too conservatively and should be loosened immediately
Nothing useful, since a calm week provides no information at all
body.explanation: Week one is genuinely useful as a functioning test: the quoting logic, inventory limits, and event playbook all worked as intended. It is not, on its own, proof of a durable edge, since Chapter 6 established that this question can only be answered once a book has actually been tested by real volatility and genuine adverse selection, which is exactly what the next lesson brings.

points: Week one ran close to the textbook version of this course's core loop: reservation-price-centred quoting, inventory staying near flat, and steady spread capture
A scheduled macro event on Thursday was handled through Chapter 4's calendar-based widening and narrowing playbook, without needing any aggressive unwind
Week one's metrics, an 83% spread capture rate, a 3.2% fill ratio, and a roughly 14-minute average holding time, closely matched the targets designed into the book's setup in the previous lesson
A calm week's good numbers confirm the system is functioning, not that the desk has a genuine, durable edge
Chapter 6's central lesson, that a real edge can only be judged once tested by stress, applies directly here and sets up exactly what the next lesson brings
The next lesson follows the same book through week two, where a genuine volatility shock finally puts the full toolkit to a real test
